items.originalTitle: Poll: Republicans have a MAGA dilemma after their midterm losses
items.author: Erin Doherty
items.title: Poll: Republicans have a MAGA dilemma after their midterm losses
items.summary: The Republican Party’s midterm wipeout has torn apart President Donald Trump’s coalition. For months, polling has shown cracks among Trump’s 2024 voters over immigration , the Iran war and the president’s influence. Now, new results from The POLITICO Poll , conducted just days after the election, reveal a deep chasm between Trump’s self-identified MAGA base and the non-MAGA voters who helped fuel his return to the White House. The two camps hold sharply different interpretations of the GOP’s historic midterm defeat and what comes next for their party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global. MAGA Trump loyalists were more likely to say the president is not to blame for the losses — that things would have gone better if he was on the ballot — and that the party should now move closer to Trump. Non-MAGA Trump voters starkly disagreed, saying they are ready to move away from him and his unpopular agenda. About one in five said they voted for Democratic candidates this cycle. The fault line is a fresh warning sign that Republicans, desperate to stitch back together a winning coalition after their midterm calamity, may struggle to keep the voters that powered Trump’s victory in 2024 in the fold. And it calls into question just how loyal the party should be to a leader — and movement — it has spent the last decade united around. Overall, just over half of all Trump voters said the president will be able to make a comeback from the election losses. “As the [GOP] spends the next two years figuring out who it is and what it stands for, these divisions will only be further exposed,” said Republican strategist Doug Heye. Here are four charts that show just how much the midterms have divided Trump’s own voters. A majority of non-MAGA Trump voters blamed Republicans' loss of the House and the Senate on Trump’s actions since taking office, with far fewer saying the campaigns themselves were responsible. A 59% majority also said the president is a loser of the midterms, a striking rebuke from a group of voters who helped his return to the White House. But MAGA Trump voters are torn over who they blame for their losses. The divide mirrors disagreements happening at the top levels of the Republican Party. In the immediate aftermath of the election, some Republicans, at least tepidly, began pointing fingers at the president. Others have called for a “reckoning” without explicitly laying the blame at Trump’s feet or articulating an alternative vision for the GOP. “There is no way to sugarcoat what happened on Election Day. From coast to coast, and in some of the reddest parts of the country, Republicans were humiliated,” 31 Republican National Committee members wrote in a letter to GOP lawmakers this week. Trump, who ahead of the midterms repeatedly urged voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot, insisted in a Truth Social post after the election that, “I JUST WASN’T ON THE BALLOT. IF I WERE, WE WOULD HAVE WON IN A LANDSLIDE!” “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement. As Republican Party leaders grapple with how to rebound from the midterms, MAGA isn’t ready to move on from Trump: They said the path forward is embracing Trump and his agenda. Non-MAGA Trump voters said the opposite — and nearly half of them think their Republican candidates should have broken with the president on the economy this cycle. “It is very clear that Election Day 2026 was an unequivocal rebuke of Donald Trump, both him personally and his policies,” said one national GOP operative who worked on midterm races, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the landscape. “MAGA needs a serious rebrand if it is going to have any success in the future.” That presents a complicated picture for Republican leaders, who will have to find a way to appeal to Trump’s fiercely loyal MAGA base without alienating the less committed voters who helped deliver his 2024 victory. On Election Night, as the scale of Republican losses was becoming clear, POLITICO asked GOP operatives who worked on midterm races whether the defeat meant it was time for Republicans to consider a new vision for the party. “How can it not be?” one person responded. It’s “the worst defeat a party has taken in 50 years.” Non-MAGA Trump voters are split over whether Trump can make a comeback after the midterms bloodbath. MAGA, however, is quite confident in the president’s abilities to do so. And collectively, Trump voters are more optimistic about the Republican Party than the president. Some key aspects of Trump’s agenda are unpopular with Americans, including his push for mass deportations, tariffs imposed on key trade partners and the war in Iran. The congressional Republicans who once supported many of those policies are now weighing whether they can distance themselves to regain voters’ trust. In an interview with “ 60 Minutes ” after the midterms, Trump admitted his party’s losses may be attributed at least in part to the Iran war and the resulting high gas prices — though he also mentioned how, in some cases, voters “didn’t like the candidates” and asserted, again, that he wasn’t on the ballot. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs and secured our border,” RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win back our majorities in 2028." As the party looks ahead to 2028, Republicans are already weighing how much the party’s next presidential nominee should carry the MAGA mantle. Some Hill Republicans are increasingly warming to the prospect of a Marco Rubio presidential bid, arguing that voters may be looking for a new direction after Trump — and Vice President JD Vance may be too closely tied to the president’s agenda. MAGA Trump voters said decisively that they prefer someone who has worked in the administration — another sign of their support for the president, and of the difficulty of changing course as a party given that loyalty. “I think everybody reserves the right to adjust. You know, learn from this,” GOP Rep. and incoming Oklahoma Sen. Kevin Hern recently told POLITICO . Asked his favorite candidate of the three he expected to run: Vance, Rubio or DeSantis, he replied with a smile: “Everybody.”

items.originalTitle: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
items.author: Ben Aitken
items.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
items.summary: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples.

items.originalTitle: ‘Walkie-talkie and paper just doesn’t cut it anymore’: FAA ground stop exposes air travel tech Delta’s CEO likens to the 1960s
items.author: Bilin Lin
items.title: ‘Walkie-talkie and paper just doesn’t cut it anymore’: FAA ground stop exposes air travel tech Delta’s CEO likens to the 1960s
items.summary: On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration made the rare decision to halt all flight departures nationwide, throwing travel plans into chaos. More than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart from U.S. airports after the order took effect. The agency lifted the ground stop more than four hours later, but two days on, airlines were still struggling to get flights moving again. FlightAware counted 9,201 canceled flights Friday , 6,698 Saturday and at least 1,956 by Sunday evening , roughly 17,850 cancellations over three days involving flights within, into or out of the U.S. Restarting the system was the easy part. Getting aircraft, crews and schedules back in sync is harder, and much of that work still runs on radios, spreadsheets and manual communication, according to Javier Vidal, co-founder and CEO of Moonware, a company that develops software to coordinate airport ground operations. “Many airlines operate flights where the plane goes to one city and then it goes to the next city and then it goes to the next city,” Vidal told Fortune . “So it’s not like there’s one big ground stop and then everything can resume normally… Those planes need to be repositioned to the right cities.” What triggered Friday’s ground stop Only two other nationwide ground stops have been ordered this century: after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and during an FAA computer system failure in January 2023 . This one was serious enough to trigger a response at the highest levels of government. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the White House Situation Room and the national security apparatus were activated, with FBI personnel also investigating, as Fortune reported on the federal response to the ground stop . Officials found no evidence of a cyberattack or other nefarious activity. Instead, officials linked the disruption to a flood of data that overwhelmed parts of the FAA’s aging telecommunications network, interfering with air traffic control communications and radar feeds. According to the FAA’s preliminary investigation , the excess data may have originated from two locations: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris had been installing a new router. The precise cause remains under investigation. The timing was striking. A day earlier, a global Microsoft outage disrupted police departments, courts, hospitals and government services around the world. Microsoft said there’s no indication the FAA’s ground stop was related to its services. Why airlines can’t simply hit restart One delayed or canceled flight can throw off an entire day’s schedule, Vidal said. Even after a plane reaches its gate, ground crews must refuel and clean it, restock food and handle baggage before it can depart again. Workers are often assigned to service multiple aircraft, so one late flight sets off another chain reaction. “If that first plane is late, then the other plane also gets late,” Vidal said. During a widespread disruption, ground crews may struggle to track what each aircraft still needs. “They don’t know what operations have already happened to the plane or what operations still need to happen to the plane,” he said. Part of the problem is that ground workers are typically assigned tasks based on scheduled arrival times, which rarely match reality. When one aircraft lands late and another arrives early, a worker assigned to both faces a conflict, and the delays cascade through the day. When hundreds of planes need servicing at once, it gets worse. Asked why the industry still relies on such outdated methods, Vidal, whose company sells software meant to replace them, said, “You know what? I ask myself the same question every day.” He attributed it partly to an “if it’s not broken, don’t fix it” mentality. “Walkie-talkie and paper just doesn’t cut it anymore,” Vidal said. The frustration with dated technology extends to the skies above the ramp. Delta CEO Ed Bastian has said air traffic controllers’ screens “look like something out of the 1960s and ’70s,” and that flying from Atlanta to New York takes longer today than when Delta launched the route in the 1950s . He has also argued that air traffic control is AI’s biggest opportunity in aviation . What the disruption could cost Airlines face expenses from repositioning aircraft, rescheduling crews and accommodating stranded passengers. Travelers lose time, miss work and face unexpected costs, while delayed cargo can disrupt businesses. Past disruptions show how expensive recovery can be. After a faulty CrowdStrike software update triggered roughly 7,000 cancellations over five days in July 2024, Delta estimated a $380 million revenue hit and $170 million in added expenses , partly offset by $50 million in fuel savings, for a net cost of about $500 million. The total financial impact of Friday’s shutdown has not yet been established. When flights should return to normal Bedford said Saturday that airlines expected to restore normal schedules by the end of Sunday. The FAA said Sunday that its system was stable, even with almost 2,000 flights still canceled and 9,000 delayed. Some carriers remained cautious. Delta Air Lines encouraged passengers with flexible plans to move their flights to Monday, Nov. 16, or later. Cancellation rates offer one gauge of recovery. About 5.2% of scheduled U.S. departures were canceled Sunday, compared with an average of 3.4% before Friday’s disruption, the Associated Press reported , citing aviation analytics firm Cirium. “This usually takes a few days to recover,” Vidal told Fortune . While he could not speak for the FAA or individual airlines, he expected operations to return to normal early this week. “I don’t think it’ll take much longer,” he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: Accidents, emotional affairs and impromptu Leonard Cohen dancing - My Wife Cries review
items.author: Phuong Le
items.title: Accidents, emotional affairs and impromptu Leonard Cohen dancing - My Wife Cries review
items.summary: Angela Schanelec’s famously uncompromising work takes on a new warmth in this sometimes playful study of everyday emotional turmoil The elliptical cinema of German film-maker Angela Schanelec is often described as uncompromising. This latest work, however, radiates a striking warmth. We see a marriage tearing at the seams, but this untethering is devoid of the usual dramatic flourishes. On an ordinary day like any another, construction worker Thomas (Vladimir Vulevic) notices a missed call from his wife, Carla (Agathe Bonitzer); when he phones back, she doesn’t pick up. The event holds little significance for the mild-mannered man; he carries on his usual chitchat with his co-workers, mundane catchups that unfold over static, tableaux-like shots. This deceptive calm is ruptured, however, when Thomas finds Carla sobbing helplessly on a park bench. A seismic change has taken hold within her: she will later confide in him of an emotional affair, and a tragic accident that leaves her emotionally unmoored. These revelations surface not through screaming matches, but by way of protracted conversations that resemble monologues rather than actual dialogue. Similar sequences recur as we are introduced to the rest of the couple’s social orbit, each of whom are wrestling with their own internal changes. There’s an enigmatic blend of theatricality and cinematic wizardry here; these wordy contemplations often occur when characters are on the move, walking, cycling or simply wandering about. There’s a subtle physicality and tactility to their inner struggles.

items.originalTitle: Everyone worries Gen Z trusts AI too much. Executives trust it over their own judgment twice as often
items.author: Dr. Colleen Batchelder
items.title: Everyone worries Gen Z trusts AI too much. Executives trust it over their own judgment twice as often
items.summary: For years, Gen Z has been cast as the generation that would rather ask ChatGPT than its own manager . New research points to a sharper divide, one that has less to do with age than with rank. The people leaning hardest on AI are the ones at the top. Executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file employees to trust AI over their own judgment, according to Charter’s AI Pulse survey of 5,002 full-time U.S. desk workers who use AI on the job. About a third of managers and executives say they trust AI more than their own judgment on work decisions, compared with 16.3% of non-managers. Executives are also more than twice as likely as workers to trust AI over a knowledgeable colleague. Gen Z, by contrast, approaches AI with some skepticism. In the Voices of Gen Z study from Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation, and GSV Ventures, a survey of 1,572 Americans ages 14 to 29, 69% of employed Gen Zers say they trust work completed without AI more than AI-assisted work. Only 3% put the most faith in work produced entirely by AI. That skepticism isn’t avoidance. The same survey found that 51% of Gen Zers use generative AI at least weekly. They just treat it as a supporting character, not the lead. The AI trust gap tracks rank more than age Brian Elliott, Charter’s executive-in-residence, who co-led the AI Pulse research , says where someone sits at the table matters more than the year they were born. “We surveyed over 5,000 AI users at work and found sharper divides by career stage than by age,” he tells Fortune . Part of it comes down to the job itself. “AI is great at summaries and high-level answers, which is much of what a leader needs, while workers deal with specifics where AI’s gaps show,” Elliott says. Executives also report more diligence: 81% say they always or usually fact-check AI output before using it, versus 71% of workers. “Executives say they fact-check AI more, but they’re also 3.3 times as likely as workers to use outputs they doubt, almost certainly because they have less fear that making a mistake might cost them their job,” Elliott says. The biggest driver, in his view, may be pressure. “Many leaders are expected to move fast and have all the answers, and AI suits the ‘seldom wrong, never in doubt’ habit many already have.” That combination, he says, “explains how you get a CFO who drops the CMO’s campaign into ChatGPT and quizzes her on it, trusting the tool over a peer who knows the context and spent weeks on the work.” It isn’t the first sign of executive faith in the technology. In 2025, SAP research shared with Fortune found that 74% of executives trusted AI more for business advice than colleagues or friends. Executive trust in AI carries higher stakes Misplaced trust in AI carries a bigger price at the top than at the entry level. When an executive leans on a flawed AI answer to decide who gets promoted, where the money goes, or how a team is restructured after a merger, employees absorb the consequences, and they didn’t get a vote. Optimism splits the same way. In Charter’s survey, 85% of executives are at least somewhat optimistic about AI’s impact on their organization, compared with 56% of employees. Younger workers’ wariness stems from institutions they feel have failed them , from schools to employers. 2027 budgets will test executive judgment Executives are finalizing next year’s budgets and AI strategies now. The open question is how many of those calls will rest on a leader’s judgment and how many on a chatbot’s general answer. Gen Z doesn’t give AI main character energy; it treats the technology as an assistant. Leaders who do the same could make 2027 a better year for the employees who live with their decisions. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.title: The Sensualist by Gary Shteyngart review – a delectable romp through life’s pleasures
items.summary: From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joy In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants. And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care.

items.originalTitle: In Hakeem Jeffries’ Rise to Speaker, Black Leaders See a Milestone—and a Test
items.author: Philip Wang
items.title: In Hakeem Jeffries’ Rise to Speaker, Black Leaders See a Milestone—and a Test
items.summary: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries speaks at a rally on extending Obamacare subsidies on the steps of the U.S. Capitol on Dec. 18, 2025, in Washington, DC. —Chip Somodevilla—Getty Images In 1870, Joseph Rainey of South Carolina became the first Black person to serve in the U.S. House. This week, current and newly elected House Democrats are poised to meet to select Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as the chamber’s first Black Speaker. It is a moment fraught with meaning and hurdles for both the New York Democrat and the larger Black community, multiple Black leaders tell TIME. They spoke of the symbolic significance of Jeffries taking on a role that puts him second in the presidential line of succession as well as the challenge of turning a breakthrough in Black representation into policies that actually improve voters’ lives. “When Martin Luther King Jr. said, ‘I have a dream,’ he's saying it's deeply rooted in the American dream, and that's the tradition that Congressman Jeffries taps into,” says Rev. Frederick Haynes, a pastor at a Black megachurch who was just elected to a U.S. House seat in Dallas . As Speaker, Jeffries will set the legislative priorities for the House and play a central role in negotiations over federal spending and policy. He will also help lead his party’s opposition against a Trump administration that has spent much of the past two years dismantling institutions intended to protect Americans’ civil rights , as well as a President who earlier this year shared a video portraying Barack and Michelle Obama as apes. Democrats are set to have their biggest majority since the opening years of Obama’s presidency. The moment carries echoes of 2008, when Obama’s election broke a racial barrier while raising expectations that Democrats would deliver economic relief and lasting change. For Rep. Jim Clyburn, a South Carolina Democrat and one of the most influential Black lawmakers in the country, Jeffries’ task is to advance the party’s agenda while maintaining the trust of his caucus. In an interview with TIME, he says the advice he’s given Jeffries is private, but describes the tenor of much of it in a single sentence: “Conduct yourself in such a way that you'll ensure that you won't be the last.” Jeffries has been teed up for this job ever since 2022, when House Democrats, then in the minority, selected him to replace Nancy Pelosi as their next leader. Long before this month’s midterm elections, he had already won the support of the Congressional Black Caucus as well as key progressive members such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Greg Casar , the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Yet some progressives remain skeptical of his selection, arguing that he is the wrong leader for the moment. Since Election Day, several incoming progressive members have said they remain uncommitted to backing Jeffries as Speaker, and some liberal groups have called for someone else to lead the chamber. Clyburn, who has been a mentor to Jeffries for years, suggests the Speaker role can often feel thankless, as so much of it involves managing different party factions and personalities without bruising egos. “You're operating behind a glass door,” he says. “Everybody thereby can see through.” Rep. James Clyburn speaks with Jeffries on Jan. 15, 2024 at Zion Baptist Church during a celebration of Martin Luther King Jr. —Tracy Glantz—The State/Tribune News Service via Getty Images In an open letter to his colleagues released earlier this month after historic wins in the midterm, Jeffries wrote that he intended to draw upon “the insights and perspectives of every single part of the Caucus in the days and weeks ahead.” But he also made clear that the expectations for him and his party are to do more than deliver messaging bills or score political points. “House Democrats must deliver dramatic change,” he wrote. Jeffries’ root in the Black church Haynes recalled first meeting Jeffries years ago and coming away impressed. It was at Cornerstone Baptist Church in Brooklyn, which Haynes regularly visited as a guest preacher. Cornerstone was an essential organizing hub for the Civil Rights Movement and had a close relationship with Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Jeffries attended the church while growing up in the Crown Heights neighborhood. “There are some people when you meet them and they're young, you know they have the ‘it’ factor,” Haynes says of Jeffries. “You know that they are hungry for knowledge. They are determined to make a difference.” Haynes is now one of several religious leaders poised to join Congress in January. Others include incoming Senators Adam Hamilton of Kansas, a lead pastor at a megachurch, and James Talarico of Texas, who is a seminarian. Haynes suggests Jeffries’ ascendance is also part of that trend, as he sees an opportunity for Jeffries to bring forth the best of the Black church tradition front and center. “Congressman Jeffries will have an opportunity to bring the moral tradition of the Black community that has believed in democracy, even when we've been victimized by a practice of democracy that was more fascist than democratic,” he says. “You cannot appreciate what it means to be black in this country without knowing that our community has always believed in democracy.” Turning representation into results Perhaps no one understands the challenges Jeffries is about to face better than Carl Heastie , who is the first Black Speaker of the New York Assembly, a role he’s held since 2015. Heastie has known Jeffries for decades, and worked with him when Jeffries was a member of the State Assembly from 2007 to 2012. Heastie says that being a speaker means balancing the roles of leader and legislator. It requires listening first to your constituents, but also to your colleagues, who are counting on you to manage both the chamber and your party’s caucus. It also means allowing his real-life experiences as a Black person to shape his decisions as both a lawmaker and speaker when appropriate, he says. He highlighted Jeffries’ work helping secure a 2010 state law involving how New York counted incarcerated people for state and local redistricting. It's a practice that disproportionately impacts the state’s Black population. The law required that incarcerated people by counted in their home communities. In the State Assembly, Jeffries led a passionate debate on why counting people where they are incarcerated, also known as prison gerrymandering , not only violates the rights of incarcerated people but also disenfranchises communities without a prison. “Hakeem to me was always one of the finer debaters on the floor,” Heastie says. “When he debated or spoke on the bill, everybody would stop what they were doing to make sure that you listened to him.” Heastie describes Jeffries’ expected promotion as more than just a moment of pride for his friend and former colleague. It suggests that, despite “terrible times and terrible dispositions,” the American dream remains very much alive. “That a Black person from Brooklyn can become the first Black Speaker in the history of this nation,” Heastie says. “I'm just so proud of him, and I can't wait.”

items.originalTitle: The resignation of Jensen Huang marks the end of an era. And not the one you think
items.author: Gill Whitehead, Vicki Nash
items.title: The resignation of Jensen Huang marks the end of an era. And not the one you think
items.summary: Just days after the American electorate delivered a sweeping midterm rebuke that materially curtailed Donald Trump’s presidential power, the independent board of Nvidia— the world’s most valuable firm for much of the year—launched an investigation into its own CEO, Jensen Huang. The board’s focus was Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. His resignation swiftly followed. In less than a week, we witnessed the core machinery of accountability brought to bear on two of the most powerful men in the world. But while the midterm outcome is being heralded as a resounding revival of healthy democracy, the Nvidia example should not be mistaken for a corporate oversight renaissance. Instead, Nvidia’s boardroom intervention may mark the end of a governance era, especially when it comes to frontier AI firms. Nvidia has a single-class share structure, meaning the CEO—who has a minority of votes at under 4% —remains accountable to an independent board. Elsewhere however, the governance guardrails for other powerful tech executives are rapidly eroding—a dismantling revealed in IPO filings—just as these companies amass unprecedented global influence. SpaceX and Anthropic’s recent filings disclose that post IPO, their founders have a majority of shareholder votes via multi-class share structures , dual-class for SpaceX, and a novel five-class system for Anthropic. Popularized by Alphabet and Meta , this shields them from short-term market pressures, and the appeal is clear: in the U.S., a record 36% of new listings in the first half of 2026 had dual-class shares. Yet by insulating the founders, ordinary shareholders lose any real say over major decisions, leaving traditional corporate accountability resting in the hands of insiders. Both companies also took advantage of stock exchange rules for ‘controlled companies.’ This allowed SpaceX to skip requirements for an independent board and gave Anthropic leeway to bypass standard rules for how its board members are chosen. Musk can only be removed from the board or his executive positions by the vote of Class B holders, of which he personally holds approximately 91.6%. To be fired, he would have to vote to fire himself. Anthropic’s novel approach features a Long-Term Benefit Trust—whose members appoint their own successors—that chooses a majority of the board. The co-founders hold 50.1% of the votes on all other matters, including appointing the rest of the board. Anthropic argues that the structure is designed to prioritize AI safety. But is also cements the power of the founders and the trust, leaving everyday public investors with no voting leverage to hold the board accountable to either the profit motive or the public benefit mandate. SpaceX has gone a step further by relocating its corporate domicile to Texas, where the law sets a much higher bar for minority shareholders to legally challenge the board in court. The state imposes a 3% shareholding requirement, which equates to over $50 billion in SpaceX stock. Taken together, these mechanisms represent a dismantling of the corporate governance levers meant to protect shareholders and society when things go wrong. And while OpenAI has yet to file, the swift 2023 reinstatement of its CEO—and the subsequent departure of several independent directors—demonstrates the sheer leverage already wielded by those at the helm. In recent months, advanced AI agents from frontier labs have broken past security controls, accessed external systems and carried out unauthorized cyber actions. As these early AI risks begin to materialize, questions about which corporate structures are best equipped to ensure AI safety and security, along with whether and how to regulate AI, are fast becoming matters of pressing public concern. This is a pivotal moment. At the industry level, current and forthcoming IPOs look set to ‘bake in’ higher-risk corporate governance arrangements, while state jurisdictions are actively exploring legal frameworks for agentic AI organizations that legitimize the complete absence of human oversight altogether. The rapid advance of frontier AI may feel inevitable, bringing boundless potential alongside incomprehensible risks. Yet in the race to build our automated future, these firms are strategically layering available federal, state, and market levers to consolidate control. Regulatory exemptions that might be appropriate in isolation to help startups scale are being combined by AI giants to escape oversight at the exact moment we need it most. No individual is infallible—whether vulnerable to error, hubris, or compromise—which is precisely why corporate guardrails are needed to mitigate the hazards of concentrated power. Politically, there is great impetus for action. American voters have just demonstrated the power of institutions that allow people to hold their leaders to account. The lawmakers they have elected must ensure that frontier AI companies cannot engineer that accountability away. Investors may choose to accept founders’ terms. The rest of us have not agreed to accept the risks. items.originalTitle: Priced out and unsure it pays off, more Gen Z students are getting in and not showing up—so colleges are cutting prices
items.author: Bilin Lin
items.title: Priced out and unsure it pays off, more Gen Z students are getting in and not showing up—so colleges are cutting prices
items.summary: For decades, getting into college meant convincing admissions officers you deserved a spot. Now some universities are doing the convincing: admitting students who haven’t applied, waiving application fees, and enlisting professors to personally recruit prospective freshmen, according to The Hechinger Report in a story also published by NPR . The shift comes as colleges prepare for a shrinking pool of traditional college-age students while more young people reconsider the four-year path. For the schools that depend on tuition, an empty seat is revenue that never arrives. An October report from Hanover Research , based on a July survey of 1,000 U.S. high school students ages 16 to 19, found that only 66% were interested in pursuing a bachelor’s degree, down from 79% in 2025. Interest in associate degrees rose from 36% to 45%. The longer-term trend points the same way. The share of high school graduates going directly to college fell from 70% in 2016 to 63% in 2024, the most recent year available, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics . That doesn’t mean enrollment is falling everywhere. Undergraduate enrollment rose 0.6% this fall, according to preliminary National Student Clearinghouse data . But with the number of U.S. high school graduates projected to fall from a record 3.9 million in 2025 to about 3.4 million a year by 2041 , according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education , many colleges face growing competition for each incoming class. Even students who commit don’t always show up Attracting enough Gen Z applicants is only part of the challenge. Colleges also have to convince the students they admit to actually enroll. The yield rate, the share of admitted students who ultimately enroll, fell on average from 32% in 2014 to 22% in 2024 at public colleges, according to federal figures cited by The Hechinger Report . Private nonprofit colleges saw a similar decline, from 24% to 18%. Even an enrollment deposit doesn’t guarantee a student will show up. Known as summer melt, the phenomenon occurs when students commit to a college but don’t enroll in the fall. Some choose another institution, while others don’t attend college at all. For the college that loses the student, both outcomes mean lost tuition revenue. Only the second means the student has left higher education altogether. At Whittier College near Los Angeles, the melt rate reached 17% this year, meaning roughly one in six students who committed ultimately didn’t show up, The Wall Street Journal reported . More students are also hedging their bets. In a Human Capital Education survey of more than 72,000 admitted students at 91 institutions, 10% placed deposits at more than one college in 2026, twice the share in 2024. Cost and doubts about value keep admitted students away A January brief published by the National College Attainment Network identified unexpected costs, unresolved financial aid, and emotional barriers such as fear of leaving home, uncertainty, and doubts about whether college is right for them as factors contributing to summer melt. Those concerns overlap with the ones that discourage students from pursuing college in the first place. Two questions loom over both decisions: whether a student can afford college, and whether the education will be worth it. In the Human Capital survey, 60% of respondents listed affordability, financial aid and net price among their five most important factors when choosing a college. Nearly three in 10 waited until they received financial aid offers before deciding where to enroll. Those worries don’t necessarily disappear after admission. Liz Colavita, director of survey research at Human Capital Education, pointed to the firm’s finding that 21% of admitted students said their families were insufficiently prepared to pay for college. An acceptance letter or deposit, she told Fortune , doesn’t resolve those financial obstacles. For some, the cost keeps them out entirely. Six percent of admitted students surveyed in 2026 said they would not attend any college that fall, up from 3% in 2025. Among those students, 51% cited an inability to afford college. Students are also reconsidering which skills will pay off in a changing job market. In Hanover’s survey , 25% said recent developments in AI have made them more interested in developing human-centered skills, and Fortune has reported on Gen Z’s growing turn toward skilled trades . “Students aren’t necessarily questioning whether education has value. They’re asking what kind of education will be valuable to them,” Colavita said. “Students want to see how their education connects to the world they’ll enter after graduation.” How colleges are trying to stop the melt Some colleges are reaching students before they apply. More than 820,000 students received proactive admission offers during the 2025–26 season through Common App’s direct admissions program . The number of participating institutions has nearly doubled, from 119 in 2024–25 to 234 in 2026–27. Making admission easier can remove some initial barriers, said Ken Anselment, senior director of enrollment strategy at Human Capital Education. But it doesn’t necessarily address concerns about affordability, whether students feel they belong, or the steps they still need to complete before arriving on campus. Georgia State University went after that last stretch. A $125,000 digital campaign targeted admitted students and their parents on platforms including Facebook, Instagram and YouTube. The messages first highlighted the university’s academic strengths and graduates’ career prospects, then shifted to reminders about enrollment requirements such as orientation registration. The university credits the campaign , which earned a CASE Circle of Excellence award, with reducing summer melt from 22% to 8%. It also attributes $3.2 million in tuition revenue to the effort. “One of the most important things colleges can do is treat the enrollment deposit not as the finish line, but as a milestone marking the beginning of another critical stage in the student’s journey,” Anselment said. He said preventing summer melt requires coordination among admissions, financial aid, student accounts, housing and advising. Colleges should monitor whether students are completing important enrollment steps and reach out when they hit obstacles, rather than discovering the problem after a student fails to show up. Discounts climb as budgets tighten Reminders and easier admissions can only go so far when students can’t afford to attend. Many colleges are leaning on financial aid instead. Private nonprofit colleges discounted an average of 57.1% of published tuition and fees for first-time, full-time undergraduates in 2025–26, up from 54.5% in 2024–25, according to preliminary estimates from a National Association of College and University Business Officers study of 258 institutions. The average discount rate for all undergraduates reached 51.3%, topping the previous peak of 50.8% in 2022–23. Some schools are going further. Whitman College in Washington state will cap tuition at 10% of parental income for students who enroll beginning in fall 2027. The aid shows up on the balance sheet. At DePaul University, rising student financial need pushed institutional aid up by nearly $15.5 million, to roughly $372 million for fiscal 2027, administrators said in October . Higher aid was one of several pressures on the university’s budget. DePaul said declining enrollment among continuing undergraduates, rather than new students, was its most significant enrollment challenge. It also said it could not afford salary increases this year. But more recruitment spending and financial aid aren’t always the answer, Anselment said. Colleges also need to consider what they’re offering, which students they’re trying to reach, and whether the price makes sense to those students. The financial consequences of missing an enrollment target also depend on scale, he said. Losing 100 freshmen would hit a college expecting 400 students very differently than one expecting 2,000. Schools must also weigh how much net tuition revenue those students would have generated against what it would have cost to educate them. “The point of diminishing returns comes when an institution spends more to enroll students without generating sufficient additional revenue,” he said. items.originalTitle: ‘I might live forever’: Inside billionaire Larry Connor’s no-email, 5-minute-block longevity routine
items.author: Emma Witman
items.title: ‘I might live forever’: Inside billionaire Larry Connor’s no-email, 5-minute-block longevity routine
items.summary: Billionaire Larry Connor’s pursuit of longevity has a sort of corporate brutality: optimize inputs, measure outputs, and delegate the rest. The 76-year-old real-estate mogul makes every second count, according to a report in The Wall Street Journal . He doesn’t touch an email inbox. Associates screen his messages, print them out, and respond on his behalf, the Journal reports. His days are carved into blocks as short as five minutes, punctuated by squash matches, yoga, and high-intensity interval sessions. Connor is part of a growing cohort of ultra-wealthy Americans pouring tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars a year into concierge doctors, biohacking retreats, and AI-driven wellness routines in pursuit of a longer, sharper life . Investors with more than $10 million in assets spend roughly four times as much on healthcare annually as less-wealthy peers, according to a 2018 UBS survey of wealthy investors , and more than half of those polled expected to reach 100. Billionaires are planning for the long haul, too. In UBS’s 2025 Billionaire Ambitions report , 44% said they expect to live significantly longer than they did a decade ago, and many are making longer-term investments and revisiting their wills as a result. Inside Connor’s 15-person health team Connor built his wealth through the Connor Group, the Ohio-based apartment investment firm he founded in 1992 with $400,000 and three properties. Today it manages about $5 billion in assets across 17 U.S. markets, according to the Connor Group . According to the Journal , roughly 15 specialists—strength coaches, yoga instructors, massage therapists, and a performance trainer who also works with NBA and NFL athletes—help Connor stay in fighting shape at his Miamisburg, Ohio, headquarters. He keeps at least three physicians on speed dial. An internal team known as the “LSC Department” (his initials) manages everything from his calendar to the 68 tests he’ll undergo at the Mayo Clinic this year, including a full-body MRI and a high-resolution brain scan. Connor has donated more than $15 million to Mayo, largely for aging research. Asked about his annual health spending, Connor initially estimated around $30,000. A team member corrected him, saying the figure was closer to six figures, not counting staff salaries. The Journal recounted one autumn evening when, after a trainer put him through treadmill intervals and two strength circuits, Connor asked for a “bonus” workout before stretching. His day had begun at 7:45 that morning; nearly 12 hours later, he was still in the office. Connor’s appetite for extremes extends well beyond the gym. In 2021 he descended to the Mariana Trench with Triton Submarines cofounder Patrick Lahey, and the following year he flew to the International Space Station on a 17-day private mission, becoming the first person to reach both the ocean’s deepest point and orbit within a year. Connor had said he planned to dive to the Titanic wreck with Lahey in 2026, three years after OceanGate’s Titan implosion killed five people. There are no public reports that he has made the trip. Beyond the gym: gene therapy and plasma swaps Other wealthy longevity chasers take a more experimental path. Tech entrepreneur Bryan Johnson , who spends a reported $2 million a year on his anti-aging regimen, has famously swapped plasma with his teenage son and 70-year-old father , a practice the FDA warns against for lack of evidence. He has also said he believes humans could become immortal by 2039 . Charlie Garcia, founder of R360, an invitation-only club for people worth more than $100 million, received two experimental gene therapies costing about $15,000 each at an Amazon longevity retreat led by biohacker Dave Asprey. None of it is FDA-approved. “I’m kind of a lab rat doing this, but I’m OK with it,” Garcia told the Journal . R360 members estimate they spend at least $200,000 a year on health, and roughly a fifth have installed hyperbaric chambers at home. What the research says works Experts aren’t convinced. S. Jay Olshansky, an emeritus professor at the University of Illinois Chicago who studies aging, told the Journal he urges caution on unproven treatments. Some of the most effective ways to extend lifespan, he noted, are also among the cheapest: eating well and exercising. Money has its limits, too. A Brown University study of more than 73,000 adults found that the wealthiest quarter of Americans had survival rates statistically equivalent to the poorest quarter in France, Germany, and the Netherlands. Connor, for his part, isn’t chasing immortality through untested injections. His approach is disciplined, measured, and relentlessly scheduled. “He’ll often say, like, ‘Hey, I might live forever,'” Ryan Ernst, who oversees Connor’s philanthropy, told the Journal . “And sometimes I think that’s what he’s kind of planning on.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
